title: Sure material, or a trap?
outcomes: Told that a position is a trap, finds the poisoned capture and its refutation
Asks what a capture opens and what the opponent can do next before taking material
Names the shape of the hidden reply: opened line, counter-threat, check in between or promotion
Takes material that is loose and safe, and declines a capture that has a concrete refutation
Says why a position with nothing to take is not a trap question

steps.text: A **trap** is a **lure** plus a **hidden reply**. The lure here was a free queen, and the hidden reply was a check followed by mate. Black's bishop left g4 and ended on d1, far from the defence of its own king. The reply exists in the position before you take. So before any capture ask two things. What does it open or take away? What can the other side do next?

[R] The pattern is named after the Sire de Légal, who is credited with playing it against Saint Brie in Paris in 1750. That attribution is recalled, not checked here, and the moves are exactly the line on the first board.

steps.text: [I] Why the knight? The knight check leaves White no time for the queen trade, and the bishop on c8 is ready to join in. [H] Promotion to a knight is rare in play, so most learners never look for it. Whenever a pawn is one step from the end, ask which piece it should become, not only whether it can queen.

**Five traps, four shapes.** [I] This sorting is ours. The f-pawn capture **opened a line**. The knight capture ignored a **counter-threat**. The captures on e7 and b4 each met a **check in between** (Bxf2+, exf2+). The last was a **promotion**: a pawn near the end is a piece in disguise. Légal combines a check with mate. Name the shape and the reply is easier to find.

steps.text: [I] Our working rule: a lure usually needs three things. It must look like a gain to someone counting material. The hidden reply must exist in *this* position: one missing piece can switch it off, as the knight on b1 showed. And the reply should come with tempo, like the check on the Nxd5 board, so the victim has no time to fix things.

steps.text: **Other voices.** Dan Heisman calls moving without checking the opponent's forcing replies "Hope Chess" (chess.com article, [S]). Nimzowitsch warned against grabbing wing pawns before development is done, but allowed a centre pawn taken without great danger (*My System*, I.i §7, our wording). Capablanca shows traps beginners fall into, the first resembling the Légal pattern [I, our reading], yet advises taking sure material. [H] Guess: club traps work because the lure looks like an even trade.

steps.prompt: Do you agree with the guess [H]? Name one capture from your own games that looked like an even trade, and what you would check now.

steps.text: **Before any capture, run two questions.** What does my capture open or take away? Which checks, captures and threats does the opponent have after it? [I] Rule of thumb: look at checks first, because they force your reply. If no forcing move hurts you, taking is usually right; the traps here were the exceptions. If one hurts, play a quiet move or work out why. Next: a safe capture with a check against it.

steps.text: **Mixed test.** From here nothing is labelled. Some positions offer sure material and taking it is the right move. Some hide a trap. One has nothing to take. Run the two questions each time, and do not treat every capture as a trap.

**What real players did** (Lichess games at 1100-1300; counts, not evaluations). Of 574 games where White's queen attacked the knight on e4, 51 retreated it to f6. Of 121 games reaching the pawn grab, 117 took it. After the f-pawn capture, 113 of 129 games recaptured with the pawn; the other 16 played something else. Of 430 games with the queen on g5, 166 chose the knight capture, and White scored 7.5% in those.

steps.text: **Recap.** A trap is a lure plus a hidden reply that your own capture made possible: an opened line, a counter-threat, a check in between, or a promotion. It works only while its pieces stand in place. Before a capture ask what it opens and which checks, captures and threats follow; if nothing, take.
